overview: This imported Shoa record covers 1279 to 1492, but its outline lies far northeast of the Shewa sites discussed here. Medieval Shewa included different Muslim, Christian and Indigenous communities. The card presents regional evidence; it does not claim that one independent kingdom ruled this entire area throughout the map interval.

periods.title: The last Makhzumi phase
periods.summary: The Muslim Shewa sultanate’s Makhzumi dynasty ended in 1285, when the Walasma established power in the region.

periods.title: Changing regional powers
periods.summary: Later Ifat towns and Christian royal centres belonged to a changing political landscape. Their evidence cannot be assigned wholesale to the earlier sultanate.

sections.title: Which Shewa are we looking at?

items.text: An Arabic chronological record describes the fall of the Makhzumi dynasty to the Walasma in 1285. Researchers still cannot securely locate the places named in those annals. The better-documented town of Nora belongs to later Ifat history, providing regional context rather than an identified old Shewa capital.

At Nora, builders used local volcanic stone: mostly rhyolite, with some cut ignimbrite blocks. They levelled house interiors and laid clay floors, moulding ovens into the clay itself. The kitchen was partly built into the floor, rather than assembled entirely from movable appliances.

Nora’s small rectangular rooms had walls roughly 40 to 50 centimetres thick. Their dimensions could support short beams beneath flat earth-covered roofs, the excavators suggest. Narrow doors, windows and wall niches made these substantial houses more than empty stone boxes.

Grinding equipment occurs throughout Nora’s archaeological levels and surrounding landscape. It points to the repeated work of processing crops. Nearby terraces and reservoirs are intriguing, but the 2024 excavation report says their medieval date remains unproved: an old-looking waterwork still needs dating.

Animal bones from Nora include cattle, sheep and goats. Butchers left cuts on some bones, and broken long bones preserve traces of food preparation. Researchers examined material from houses and a rubbish heap: yesterday’s discarded scraps can become tomorrow’s evidence about dinner.

Some cattle lived long enough to develop heavily worn teeth. The animal specialist suggests they may have supplied milk or traction before slaughter. A cow could therefore contribute much more than meat, although the bones alone cannot tell us which household milked it or what it pulled.

Beside a small Nora mosque stood a large basalt stone. Archaeologist Stéphane Pradines interprets it as a footrest used during washing before prayer, comparing similar arrangements elsewhere. This is a specific proposed use for a surviving object, not proof of a fully excavated public bathhouse.

The same mosque’s prayer room measured about 19 square metres and had a central column supporting its roof. It served worship on a much more intimate scale than a vast cathedral. Its courtyard and carefully arranged entrances show how a small building could organize communal activity.

In the Christian kingdom, royal camps could contain separate areas for the ruler’s household, soldiers, officials and livestock, sometimes divided by palisades. Researchers have explored a possible fifteenth-century royal camp in Menz, northeastern Shewa. A travelling court required space for both political business and animals.

sections.title: Beads, families and words that survive

items.text: Shay communities lived in this wider region from about the ninth to fourteenth centuries. At Meshala Maryam, a burial mound contained human remains, pottery, beads and metal ornaments. Repeated use suggests a family tomb. Their distinct burial traditions should not automatically be labelled Christian or Muslim because of nearby states.

A 2023 study analysed 34 glass beads from two Shay burial sites. Their chemistry connects the glass with several manufacturing traditions, including the Middle East, Egypt and the Indian Ocean world. Tiny ornaments reveal wide trading connections, even when the route taken by a particular bead remains unknown.

“هذا قبر” means “This is the tomb.” These Arabic words open the published transcription of tomb T9 at Awfat, dated April to May 1364. The inscription commemorates a religious scholar associated with the Walasma. It is a later Ifat writing sample in regional context, not a Makhzumi royal document.

ending.text: The old Muslim Shewa dynasty ended in 1285, but this imported record extends to 1492 without a securely identified corresponding fall. Regional communities continued under changing powers. Nora’s excavated urban history itself reaches into the early sixteenth century, so 1492 should not erase its inhabitants.
